name: Hormonal Hair Loss

description: Estrogen, thyroid hormone, DHT and cortisol matter most for hair growth. What each does, what happens when it shifts, and how we read it in Atlanta.
h1: Which Hormones Control Hair Growth, and What Happens When They Shift
subtitle: Four hormones do most of the work. When they move, your hair reports it.

hero.alt: 200x view of hairs of mixed thickness at the crown
hero.caption: Mixed thickness side by side, at 200x.

quickAnswer: Four hormones do most of the work in hair growth: estrogen, thyroid hormone, DHT and cortisol. Estrogen holds hair in its growth phase, which is why hair often feels thickest in pregnancy and thinner after birth or through menopause. Thyroid hormone sets the pace of the growth cycle, so both an underactive and an overactive thyroid can cause shedding. DHT, a derivative of testosterone, shrinks sensitive follicles at the crown and temples over time. Cortisol, your stress hormone, pushes hairs out of growth and into shedding early. Hormonal hair loss usually looks like diffuse thinning through the top and a widening part rather than a bald patch. At Nina Ross Atlanta in Sandy Springs we read your scalp at 200x and look at the systems behind it. Serving all of Metro Atlanta.

items.title: Estrogen shifts
items.text: Postpartum, perimenopause and menopause all lower estrogen support for the growth phase, so more hairs enter shedding at the same time.

items.title: Thyroid function
items.text: Both underactive and overactive thyroid disrupt the growth cycle. Thyroid-related shedding is diffuse rather than patchy.

items.title: DHT sensitivity
items.text: DHT miniaturizes sensitive follicles. Inherited sensitivity, more than the amount of hormone alone, determines who thins.

items.title: Cortisol and chronic stress
items.text: Sustained cortisol pushes follicles out of growth early. It shows up as a shedding wave a few months after the stressful period.{cite:1}

insight.kicker: What we see that others miss
insight.title: Reading hormonal thinning at 200x
paras: Hormonal thinning has a signature under magnification: hairs of noticeably different thicknesses sitting side by side in the same area, which is called variability in shaft caliber. That single finding separates hormonal miniaturization from a plain shedding episode, where the hairs that remain are all still full thickness.

faq.q: Which hormone is most responsible for hair loss?
faq.a: There is no single one. For thinning at the crown and temples, DHT sensitivity leads. For sudden shedding, thyroid, estrogen and cortisol are the usual suspects. Which one is driving yours is what we are looking for.

faq.q: Will it grow back if my hormones settle?
faq.a: Shedding usually settles once the trigger passes, and follicles producing finer hair can often be supported back toward thicker hair when the driver is addressed. How much returns depends on the stage we see at 200x. Results not typical. Individual results will vary.
Sometimes. If your scalp read and history point to a hormonal or nutrient driver, testing helps confirm which one, and that work happens in-house.

faq.q: Is hormonal thinning different in Black women?
faq.a: The hormones work the same way. What differs is how often a widening part gets blamed on styling. We read tension and hormonal patterns as separate findings and tell you which one your scalp is showing.

faq.q: How long before I can tell anything is changing?
faq.a: Hair grows slowly, so change takes months to see. We photograph the same points each visit, so you compare against your own baseline instead of a memory.
